content: When co-administering drugs that are substrates of OCT2 or MATE transporters, avoid such combinations if possible. If co-administration is unavoidable, monitor for toxicities related to the substrate drug and consider reducing its dosage based on the product labeling of the co-administered drug. Tecovirimat can reduce the levels or effects of trimethoprim by influencing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. As tecovirimat is a weak CYP3A4 inducer, monitor the effectiveness of sensitive CYP3A4 substrates when co-administered. Additionally, tecovirimat and trimethoprim both increase the QTc interval, so close monitoring is required. Similarly, trimethoprim and telmisartan both elevate serum potassium levels, necessitating caution and monitoring. Trimethoprim decreases urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia, especially at high doses, in patients with renal insufficiency, or when combined with other hyperkalemia-inducing drugs. Trimethoprim can reduce thiamine levels or effects by altering intestinal flora, but this interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents and is of minor or unknown significance. Thioridazine and trimethoprim both increase the QTc interval, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Trimethoprim increases the levels or effects of tovorafenib by reducing its metabolism, making co-administration with strong or moderate CYP2C8 inhibitors inadvisable. Avoid or use alternative drugs in such cases. Trimethoprim and trandolapril both elevate serum potassium levels, necessitating caution and monitoring. Trimethoprim also interacts with triamterene, increasing serum potassium levels and potentially causing hyperkalemia. Triamterene may increase trimethoprim levels due to competition for renal tubular clearance, though the mechanism is unspecified and of minor or unknown significance. Hyperkalemia remains a concern in such combinations. Trimethoprim and trifluoperazine both prolong the QTc interval, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Trilaciclib decreases trimethoprim levels or effects, and co-administration with OCT2, MATE1, or MATE-2K substrates should be avoided due to the risk of serious or life-threatening toxicities. Trimipramine and trimethoprim both increase the QTc interval, necessitating therapy modification and close monitoring. Tropisetron and trimethoprim also prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and monitoring. Trimethoprim increases the levels or effects of tucatinib, and tucatinib can elevate trimethoprim levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with CYP3A substrates should be avoided, as even minimal concentration changes may lead to serious toxicities. If unavoidable, reduce the CYP3A substrate dose according to product labeling. Trimethoprim reduces the effects of live typhoid vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism, making co-administration contraindicated. Wait until antibiotic therapy is complete before administering live bacterial vaccines. Valsartan and trimethoprim both increase serum potassium levels, requiring caution and monitoring. Trimethoprim and venlafaxine both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating caution and monitoring. Trimethoprim may increase verapamil levels due to competition for renal tubular clearance, though this interaction is of minor or unknown significance. Voclosporin and trimethoprim both decrease serum potassium levels, requiring caution and monitoring. Voriconazole and trimethoprim both prolong the QTc interval, necessitating caution and monitoring. Trimethoprim increases zidovudine levels by reducing renal clearance, potentially increasing toxicity. Monitor closely in such cases. Ziprasidone and trimethoprim both prolong the QTc interval, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Adverse effects of trimethoprim include aseptic meningitis, fever, maculopapular rash (3-7% incidence at 200 mg/day, higher with larger doses), erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, pruritus (common), phototoxic skin eruptions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, epigastric distress, glossitis, nausea, vomiting, leukopenia, megaloblastic anemia, methemoglobinemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, liver enzyme elevation, cholestatic jaundice, increased BUN and creatinine, anaphylaxis, and hypersensitivity reactions. Prolonged use may interfere with hematopoiesis, with early signs such as sore throat, fever, pallor, or purpura indicating serious blood disorders. Monitor for hematologic disorders and discontinue the drug if significant reductions in blood cell counts are observed. Prolonged use may also lead to fungal or bacterial superinfections, including Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis, which can occur more than two months after antibiotic treatment. Use caution in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, as well as those at risk of folate deficiency (e.g., malnourished individuals, those on chronic anticonvulsant therapy, or the elderly). Folates may be administered concomitantly without interfering with the antibacterial action of trimethoprim. Some dosage forms may contain benzyl alcohol, which should be avoided in neonates. Trimethoprim is not indicated for prophylactic or prolonged use in otitis media at any age. During pregnancy, trimethoprim is classified as Category C, and it enters breast milk. It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, thereby inhibiting folic acid reduction to tetrahydrofolate, which suppresses microorganism growth. It is readily absorbed, with a serum peak time of 1-4 hours, and distributes widely into body tissues and fluids, including the middle ear, prostate, bile, aqueous humor, and cerebrospinal fluid. It crosses the placenta and enters breast milk. Protein binding is 42-46%, and it is partially metabolized hepatically. The half-life is 8-14 hours but is prolonged in renal impairment. Excretion occurs primarily via urine (60-80%) as unchanged drug.
